evals.prompt: I have the titanic passenger data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. I want to fit a logistic regression predicting survival (Yes/No) from pclass, sex, and age, and walk through interpreting the odds ratios. I'm new to logistic regression.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py (or its Python equivalent), finds and reads titanic_description.md to learn the variable meanings (pclass is socioeconomic proxy, sex is female/male, age in years). Picks lev='Yes' for the positive outcome (modeling P(survived = Yes)) and explicitly confirms with the user. Fits with rsm.model.logistic({'titanic': df}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=['pclass', 'sex', 'age']), prints summary(), and walks through: (1) the model setup (logistic regression on titanic, modeling P(survived=Yes)); (2) overall fit — chi-squared ≈ 428.26 on 4 df, p < .001 → model is significant overall; pseudo R² (McFadden) ≈ 0.30 (good for marketing/business work, not directly comparable to linear R²); AUC ≈ 0.84 → the model correctly ranks 84% of random survivor/non-survivor pairs; (3) each odds-ratio interpretation with sidecar units: pclass[2nd] OR=0.28, OR%=-72% → 'compared to 1st-class passengers, 2nd-class passengers had 72% lower odds of survival, holding sex and age constant'; pclass[3rd] -89.8% lower odds; sex[male] OR=0.083, -91.7% lower odds vs. female; age OR=0.966, -3.4% lower odds per additional year. (4) explicitly mentions the 'do not rank predictors by OR magnitude' rule and points to permutation importance (Step 9) as the right way to compare predictor importance. (5) optionally offers to run clf.plot('or') for a forest plot of the odds ratios with CIs.

evals.prompt: Same titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Now my manager wants the business-decision metrics: confusion matrix, AUC, profit at margin=$10 cost=$1 per contact, and a gains chart. Walk me through evaluating classification performance.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: refits or re-uses the previous logistic model, then runs the perf submodule workflow inline. (1) Attaches predictions to the data: pred = clf.predict(); data_with_pred = clf.data.with_columns(pl.Series('prediction', pred['prediction'])). (2) Computes evalbin: rsm.model.perf.evalbin(data_with_pred, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', pred='prediction', cost=1, margin=10) — prints the one-row DataFrame with TP, FP, TN, FN, precision, recall, F1, AUC, profit, ROME, contact rate. Walks through key cells with substantive business interpretation. (3) For the confusion matrix specifically, uses rsm.model.perf.confusion(...) and reports the (TP, FP, TN, FN, contact) tuple, explicitly stating that this is at the PROFIT-MAX THRESHOLD (not a default 0.5) — explains that profit_max chooses the cutoff probability that maximizes margin * P(success) - cost given the user's cost/margin. (4) States the AUC ≈ 0.84 with interpretation. (5) Computes profit_max separately to get the max profit value: rsm.model.perf.profit_max(data_with_pred, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', pred='prediction', cost=1, margin=10). (6) Runs gains_plot and gains_tab to produce the cumulative-gains chart and the 10-decile table — interprets: 'by contacting the top X% by predicted probability we capture Y% of actual survivors'. (7) IMPORTANTLY: explicitly states cost=$1 and margin=$10 in every profit-related interpretation since these are user-supplied business parameters that change the optimal threshold and profit. (8) Optionally also calls lift_plot for the lift chart and ROME_plot for the ROI-per-dollar view. (9) Adds the important caveat that these metrics are computed on the TRAINING data — for an honest deployment estimate, the user should split with rsm.model.make_train, fit on training, then evaluate on test.

evals.prompt: I fit the same logistic regression on /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet (survived ~ pclass + sex + age). Looking at the z-values, age has |z| = 5.44 but sex has |z| = 14.996. Does that mean sex is roughly 3x more important than age in this model? My TA said to compare z-values for importance.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) pushes back on using z-values (or odds ratios) to rank predictor importance — this is the explicit critical concept the skill is designed to surface. (2) Explains why: (a) z-values reflect the precision of the coefficient estimate, not the magnitude of the effect on outcome ranking. A predictor with a tiny but very precisely-estimated effect can have a huge |z| while contributing little to AUC. (b) Odds ratios are on different scales for numeric vs. categorical predictors and for predictors with different ranges (a 1-year change in age is incomparable to a 1-level change in sex). Comparing them as 'importance' is a category error. (3) Recommends the correct approach: permutation importance via clf.plot('pip', ret=True). Runs it and reports the actual results: sex (importance ≈ 0.215, the largest AUC drop when permuted) > pclass (≈ 0.089) > age (≈ 0.028). (4) Translates: 'permutation importance shuffles each predictor and measures the resulting drop in AUC. A larger drop = more important predictor for the model's discrimination. By this measure, sex is the most important (AUC drops by ≈0.22 without it), pclass is second (≈0.09 drop), age is third (≈0.03 drop) — broadly consistent with the directional intuition from the odds ratios but on a comparable, model-agnostic scale'. (5) Refuses to provide a '3x more important' headline number from z-values or odds ratios — the right comparison comes from permutation importance, which is roughly 'sex contributes ~2.4x more to the model's discrimination than pclass and ~7.7x more than age' if you want a multiplicative reading. (6) Optionally suggests further: for a clean interpretation, also report effect sizes in plain-English terms (an 'average' male-vs-female effect on survival probability, holding pclass and age at their modes/means) using clf.predict(cmd={'sex': ['female', 'male']}). (7) Re-emphasizes the broader principle: 'always report permutation importance when asked to rank predictors. Odds ratios and z-values answer different questions and don't translate to importance rankings.'
